# Umbraco Rules

Project conventions, enforced by code in `Umbraco.Bench.Umbraco` where possible. The short version of the ten UmbraCommandments.

1. **Never put content behind a composition.** Removing a composition permanently deletes its content on every document that used it — no recovery through revisions. Compositions are for meta, settings, CTAs. Litmus test: *if we remove this composition later, is what remains still viable content?*
2. **There are six kinds of document type — file each in its folder.** Page (renders), Block (renders; lives in block list/grid; never used as a composition), Composition (composed onto others; never rendered, never pickable), Data (element; never renders — settings, events, people), Repository (container node; never renders), Repository Item (the pickable records inside a Repository).
3. **Data types never sit at the root of the data type tree.** Built-ins under `/Umbraco/<editor>`, custom ones under `/Custom/<editor>`. `DataTypeSavedHandler` enforces this on every save.
4. **Register in an `IComposer`, not Program.cs.** If `IUmbracoBuilder` can do it, it belongs in `Composers/`. Non-Umbraco concerns (CORS, App Insights) go in `WebApplicationBuilder` extension methods.
5. **Production runs in production mode.** Umbraco Application Url set, `--configuration Release`, HTTPS only, no model generation, no template editing. `appsettings.json` ships configured this way — don't soften it; put dev conveniences in `appsettings.Development.json`.
6. **Aliases are English and camelCase.** No exceptions.
7. **Dictionary keys are PascalCase with dots** (`My.Dictionary.Item`), and a dictionary folder never has values of its own.
8. **Media always lives in a folder.**
9. **The content root only holds Repositories.** The site hangs under the WWW `siteRoot` node; going multi-site means adding another Page beneath it, not re-architecting. Because WWW never renders, the site Page needs a **domain** or nothing answers on `/` — assign `/` for a single site, a hostname each for several.
10. **uSync everything — commit `Umbraco.Bench.Umbraco/uSync/`.** Export is automatic; you should not need to trigger it. On Umbraco Cloud, use Umbraco Deploy instead.

input.name: One Protocol, Every Tool: Why MCP Is Awesome

values.value: Before MCP, every AI integration was a bespoke adapter. The Model Context Protocol replaces that tangle with one open standard, and the difference is hard to overstate.

value.markup:
The end of one-off integrations

Connecting an AI assistant to a system used to mean writing a custom plugin for that exact assistant and that exact system. Ten assistants and ten systems meant a hundred adapters, each with its own quirks and its own way of breaking.

The Model Context Protocol, or MCP, flips that around. A system describes what it can do once, as a set of tools with typed inputs and outputs, and any MCP-aware client can discover and use them. You build the integration once and every client benefits.

values.value: One standard plug, many devices. Photo: Hal Gatewood on Unsplash.

value.markup:
Discoverable by design

An MCP server tells the client what it offers. There is no documentation to paste into a prompt and no endpoint list to memorise: the assistant asks the server for its tools, reads their schemas, and works out how to call them.

That is how this very post got into the CMS. The assistant listed the document types, looked up the data types it needed, created the content and published it, all through tools the Umbraco MCP server advertised about itself.

  • Typed inputs mean fewer malformed calls.
  • Self-describing tools mean no stale documentation.
  • An open standard means no vendor lock-in.

input.name: MCP Turns Your CMS into Something an AI Can Work In

values.value: A CMS has always been a place where humans click through forms. With an MCP server it becomes a place where an assistant can model, create and verify content, with you reviewing the result.

value.markup:
From forms to conversations

Content management has always meant clicking through forms: create a document type, add a property, pick a data type, save, repeat. It works, but it is slow when the task is really just describing what you want.

With the Umbraco MCP server, an assistant can do those steps for you. It can create element types, wire them into a block grid, import media, and publish pages. You describe the site; it does the clicking.

values.value: Pieces that fit together because they share an interface. Photo: Vardan Papikyan on Unsplash.

value.markup:
Safe, because it is the same API

The MCP server does not bypass anything. It talks to the same management API the backoffice uses, with the same permissions, validation and audit trail. A change made by an assistant is a change you can see, review and roll back like any other.

Better still, every structural change can be read straight back. Create a document, fetch it again, and confirm the content landed exactly as intended before moving on.

  • Model: document types, element types, data types and templates.
  • Create: documents, media and domains.
  • Verify: read everything back through the same tools.

Connecting an AI assistant to a system used to mean writing a custom plugin for that exact assistant and that exact system. Ten assistants and ten systems meant a hundred adapters, each with its own quirks and its own way of breaking.

I built a simple blog and it renders correctly. I fetched the front page, both posts, an image and the CSS over HTTPS and got 200s with the expected content. I haven't looked at it in a browser.

**How to view it:** the site is running now at https://localhost:44317/. To restart it, run `cd Umbraco.Bench.Umbraco && dotnet run`. The backoffice login is admin@example.com / 1234567890.

**What I built, all through the Umbraco MCP server and in the order you gave:**
- **Modeling:**
  - **Blocks:** five block types (`heroBlock`, `richTextBlock`, `imageBlock`, `quoteBlock`, `blogPostListBlock`) in the Blocks folder.
  - **Pages:** `blogFrontPage` and `blogPost` in Pages, each with its own template.
  - **Block grids:** two block grid data types, "Blog Front Page Blocks" and "Blog Post Blocks". `DataTypeSavedHandler` filed them under `/Custom/`.
  - **Allowed children:** `siteRoot` allows `blogFrontPage`, and `blogFrontPage` allows `blogPost`.
- **Content:**
  - **Front page:** "MCP Blog" sits under WWW with the domain `/`. It has a hero block and a "Latest posts" list block.
  - **Posts:** "One Protocol, Every Tool: Why MCP Is Awesome" and "MCP Turns Your CMS into Something an AI Can Work In". Each has a hero image and a block grid of rich text, image and quote blocks.
  - **Images:** six Unsplash photos imported into a "Blog" media folder. The photographer credits are in the image captions.
- **Razor, written after the restart:**
  - **Rendering:** pages call `Html.GetBlockGridHtmlAsync`, and each block has an adapter in `Views/Partials/blockgrid/Components/<alias>.cshtml`. The adapter builds a plain model (in `Models/Blocks/`) and invokes a ViewComponent. The markup lives in `Views/Shared/Components/<Name>/Default.cshtml`.
  - **Support files:** a shared `_Layout.cshtml` and an updated `_ViewImports.cshtml`.
  - **Frontend:** I ran `npm install` and `npm run build` in `Umbraco.Bench.Frontend` to generate the Tailwind CSS in `wwwroot/dist`.

I didn't write any migrations.

**Known issues:**
- The front page `<title>` reads "The MCP Blog – The MCP Blog", because the layout appends the site name to a page title that already is the site name.
- `dotnet build` shows one nullable-reference warning in `blogPostListBlock.cshtml`. It doesn't affect the output.
- `_ViewImports.cshtml` pointed at the `Umbraco.Cms.Web.Common.PublishedModels` namespace, but the generated models use `Umbraco.Bench.Umbraco.Models`. I switched the import to match.
- My first attempt to create the Razor files in one shell script failed on a syntax error and wrote nothing. I redid them as individual file writes.
- I couldn't commit the `uSync/` folder because the project isn't a git repository.
